questions.section: Why aircraft look the way they do
questions.question: A team sets its configuration by engineering judgment at the start of conceptual design. What is the status of that configuration?
options: An initial choice that the analysis has to confirm
A final choice, since judgment replaces analysis here
A choice free of compromise, if it meets the requirements
A choice set by existing aircraft, not by the requirements
questions.explanation: Judgment starts the design, and only the analysis shows whether the configuration meets the requirements. Requirements drive the choice, and every choice is a compromise.

questions.question: A design changes from a high wing to a low wing. What does the change bring?
options: Shorter gear and a need for dihedral
Longer gear and a need for dihedral
Shorter gear and, usually, a T-tail
Longer gear and easier loading
questions.explanation: A low wing gains short gear and a spar under the cabin, and it requires dihedral. Long or podded gear, a T-tail, and easy loading belong to the high wing.

questions.question: A fuselage changes from a circular cross-section to a chined or blended one. What does the change bring?
options: More fuselage lift and harder pressurization
More fuselage lift and easier construction
Less fuselage lift and harder pressurization
Lower drag and better use of volume
questions.explanation: A chined or blended section gains fuselage lift and lower drag. It pays with difficult construction, poor volume use, and hard pressurization, the three things a circular section does well.

questions.question: A design moves its engines from pods under the wing to pods on the aft fuselage. What does the change bring?
options: A clean wing and, usually, a T-tail
Wing bending relief and a quieter cabin
Longer gear and weight farther forward
No nacelle drag and a duct that loses pressure
questions.explanation: Aft-fuselage pods give a clean wing, a quiet cabin, and short gear, and they cost aft weight and usually a T-tail. Bending relief comes from pods under the wing, and a duct that loses pressure belongs to a buried engine.

questions.question: A V-tail is sized so that its projected areas equal the areas of the horizontal and vertical tails it replaces. How does that sizing turn out?
options: Too small, because a V-tail needs more area than its projection
Too large, because a V-tail has less area than the tails it replaces
Correct, because the projected areas do the work of the two tails
Correct in area, but exposed to deep stall like a T-tail
questions.explanation: A V-tail is meant to save area and drag, but it needs more area than its projection suggests. Sizing by projection alone leaves the tail undersized.

questions.question: A team adds a canard concept to its candidates and claims an advantage for it. How is that claim treated in the selection?
options: Scored against a requirement in the Pugh matrix
Accepted without scoring, since published aircraft show it
Dropped before the matrix, since the concept is unconventional
Given a bonus in the matrix for originality
questions.explanation: Unconventional options enter the Pugh matrix like any other. Each claimed advantage is scored against a requirement, with no bonus and no penalty for being unusual.

questions.question: Bicycle, single main, and quadricycle gear each save fuselage width, weight, or gear length. What cost do all three carry?
options: Difficult or no rotation
A heavy nose gear
A wider fuselage
A large and complex gear
questions.explanation: The gear must allow rotation. The bicycle and the quadricycle make it difficult, and the single main gives none.

questions.question: A morphological chart has five rows and three options in each row. How many configurations can be composed from it, before any is disqualified?
questions.explanation: One pick per row is a configuration, which gives 3 × 3 × 3 × 3 × 3 = 3<sup>5</sup> = 243. Fifteen is the number of options in the chart.
